tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed paper (IEEE TPDS 2021, arXiv 2004.10908). In its abstract and Section 7.4 it reports up to 29% faster runtime, 1.5x less memory, and 1.9x higher corun throughput than oneTBB FlowGraph on LSDNN inference. The full text states clang++ v10 with -O2, but the CPU is only '40 Intel Xeon CPU cores at 2.00 GHz' with no model number, and public code for the LSDNN experiment was not confirmed, so the record falls short of A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang++ v10 as the host compiler under Nvidia CUDA v11, -std=c++17 -O2 (paper says no significant difference vs -O3)
corrections.hardware: 40 Intel Xeon CPU cores at 2.00 GHz (exact model not stated), 4 GeForce RTX 2080 GPUs, 256 GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux 5.0.0-21-generic
corrections.workload: MIT/Amazon Large Sparse Deep Neural Network (LSDNN) Inference Challenge: 1920-layer sparse DNN (4096 or 65536 neurons per layer) run as a heterogeneous CPU+GPU task graph (up to 4 cudaFlows) by Taskflow vs oneTBB (2021.1) FlowGraph and StarPU. Throughput is weighted speedup across up to 9 co-running processes on 40 CPUs and 4 GPUs.
corrections.caveats: This benchmark measures Taskflow against Intel oneTBB FlowGraph (and StarPU, HPX, OpenMP), not against std::async/std::thread/std::future directly. oneTBB is already catalogued separately, so this result shows Taskflow beating another fast library, one step removed from the std baseline. The 1.9x throughput figure is the best case (5 co-runs, 1920x4096 network); memory use is 1.5-1.7x lower than oneTBB and StarPU. The paper states clang++ v10 -O2 but not the exact Xeon model, and public code for the LSDNN experiment was not confirmed, so the record is tier B, not A. GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the standard MIT text (headed 'TASKFLOW MIT LICENSE'). The repo's benchmarks/ directory compares Taskflow to OpenMP tasking and TBB FlowGraph, not to std::async/std::thread.

notes: The claim matches the paper's abstract verbatim. The full paper supplies the compiler, flags, and generic hardware that the record had left null. The LICENSE file is MIT; 12,183 stars and last commit 2026-09-14 were checked and are correct.

tier_reason: Upgraded from B to A. The paper (SPIRE 2022, arXiv 2206.01149) compares pasta-flat/pasta-poppy directly against cs-poppy and cs-poppy-fs. It states GCC 10.2 with -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG on an AMD Ryzen 9 3950X. The reproduction code is public at github.com/pasta-toolbox/bit_vector_experiments (run_benchmarks.sh).

corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (16 cores, up to 3.5 GHz), 64 GiB DDR4 RAM, Ubuntu 20.04.2 LTS; single core used (sequential experiments)
corrections.caveats: std::bitset and std::vector<bool> have no native rank/select, so there is no direct std baseline for this functionality. The recorded baseline (cs-poppy, Zhou et al. SEA'13) is the field's standard compact rank/select structure, not a stdlib facility, which caps confidence. The gains are small: rank is roughly 8% faster (pasta-poppy and pasta-flat) and select is 16.5% faster (pasta-flatSIMD) vs cs-poppy at the same ~3.51% space overhead. Rank-only structures such as sdsl-v and rank9select answer rank faster but use 1.75-6.98x more space. The paper is peer-reviewed (SPIRE 2022, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-20643-6_19), and reproduction scripts are public at github.com/pasta-toolbox/bit_vector_experiments. GPL-3.0 is a copyleft license.

notes: The 8%/16.5% numbers and the 3.51% overhead appear in the abstract and the evaluation section. The full-text experimental setup provides the compiler, flags, and CPU model, so the tier moves from B to A. GPL-3.0, 36 stars, and last commit 2025-04-07 (stale) were checked and are correct.
